I will keep to the wheat-maize rotation on my land this year. In Quzhou, that is still the steadiest way for me to make use of the full year, and at my age I want a system I know well, can manage with ordinary machinery, and can sell easily. I will not chase too many crops. I would rather plant what matches the local weather, my soil, and my labor strength. So I will finish the winter wheat already in the ground, then after harvest I will go straight into summer maize on the same fields.

For wheat, I will use an improved local variety because I trust its stability more than anything fancy. I will put fertilizer in at a moderate level, not too light and not too aggressive, because I want steady yield without wasting money. I will irrigate mainly at the key stages, especially around jointing and grain filling if water allows. I will keep pesticide use limited to what is needed for aphids, rust, or other common problems. After wheat harvest, I will seed hybrid summer maize quickly so I do not lose soil moisture or the season. For maize, I will use no-tillage direct seeding after wheat because it saves labor and time, which matters to me. I will feed maize a bit heavier on nitrogen than wheat, watch for armyworm and corn borer, and irrigate at the main demand stages if rain is short. This is the plan I would choose because it is familiar, practical, and gives me the best balance of risk, work, and output.
